column4: The server always renders the default language regardless of the visitor language cookie
column5: Requested against a running dev server with the language cookie i18nextLng set to ar and then to en the /categories/ page returns IDENTICAL English output - zero Arabic characters appear in the server HTML in either case - even though that page explicitly awaits loadTranslations(context) at src/pages/categories/index.tsx:179. The cookie name is correct: i18n.ts:12 defines LANGUAGE_KEY as i18nextLng and loadTranslations reads it at :58-59 and passes it as lng to i18n.init at :62-69. The reason it has no effect is that the i18next singleton is ALREADY initialised at module scope - i18n.ts:29 runs i18n.use(initReactI18next).init({...}) when the module is first imported - and calling init again on an initialised instance does not switch the active language. The API that does is changeLanguage which the same file already uses at :45 for the client side switch. So every server rendered page is produced in the default language and the correct language is applied only after hydration.
column9: Any visitor whose language is Hindi or Arabic requesting any server rendered page.
column10: 1. Set the cookie i18nextLng to ar. 2. Request /categories/ and read the raw HTML before JavaScript runs. 3. Compare it against the same request with i18nextLng set to en - the two are identical.
column11: The server renders the page in the visitor language so the first paint is already correct.
column12: Both locales receive the same English HTML and the language is corrected only after the client hydrates.
column13: Hindi and Arabic customers see a full English page on first paint that then swaps which is visible on every navigation and worst on slow connections. Search engines only ever receive English so every localised page is indexed as English which undermines localised search entirely. It also compounds defect 12 - the document declares lang en - so the server response is consistently English in both content and markup.
column14: Call i18n.changeLanguage(lang) inside loadTranslations rather than relying on a second init - and await it so the resources are active before the page renders. Verify by requesting a page with each locale cookie and confirming the served HTML differs.

column4: The html element declares English and carries no direction for every visitor
column5: Requested against a running dev server with the language cookie set to en and then hi and then ar the served document is <html lang="en" prefix="og: https://ogp.me/ns#"> in all three cases - the lang value never changes and there is no dir attribute at all. src/pages/_document.tsx:5 hard-codes lang to the literal string en and nothing in the document sets dir. The correction happens only in the browser - src/pages/_app.tsx:58-62 sets both attributes on documentElement once the language is known - so anything reading the response before hydration sees English left to right. Confirms code review issue 47 by observation across all three locales.
column9: Any Hindi or Arabic visitor and any crawler or assistive technology reading the initial response.
column10: 1. Request any page with the cookie i18nextLng set to ar. 2. Read the html element in the raw response before JavaScript runs.
column11: The document declares the visitor language and direction.
column12: It declares lang en and carries no dir for every locale.
column13: Screen readers may apply English pronunciation to Arabic and Hindi content read during load - search engines see every localised page as English - and Arabic users get a left to right first paint that flips after hydration. Together with defect 11 the entire server response is English in both markup and content.
column14: Read the locale from the request in _document getInitialProps and set lang and dir on the Html element server side - keeping the existing _app effect for in session language changes.

column4: The storefront serves Figtree while the documented and redesign target is Plus Jakarta Sans
column5: Requested against a running dev server the home page loads fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Figtree through a stylesheet link and the served HTML contains zero occurrences of Jakarta. CLAUDE.md states in three places that the storefront sans is Plus Jakarta Sans loaded through next/font/google in src/config/fonts.ts - the tech stack table in section 2 - the redesign token block - and section 9 rule 13 which adds that Figtree remains only as the mono fallback. The redesign notes list Figtree among the stale values that must not be reintroduced and section 6.7 makes the typeface an explicit visual regression check. The shipped chain is tailwind.config.ts:20 mapping sans to var(--font-sans) - src/styles/globals.css:304 defining that variable as Figtree - and src/pages/_document.tsx:16-27 pulling Figtree from Google Fonts with a comment calling it the site sans typeface. Confirms code review issue 43 by observation.
column9: Every page - the typeface is global.
column10: 1. Load any page. 2. Inspect the font-family resolved on body or read the stylesheet link in the head. 3. Search the response for Jakarta.
column11: Text renders in Plus Jakarta Sans loaded through next/font/google as the documentation and the redesign target require.
column12: Every screen renders in Figtree and Plus Jakarta Sans is never loaded.
column13: Every screen diverges from its redesign twin on letterforms and weights and vertical rhythm so the reskin does not match its own pixel target. The Google Fonts stylesheet is also render blocking and needs two extra preconnects that next/font/google would remove.
column14: Load Plus Jakarta Sans through next/font/google in src/config/fonts.ts at weights 400 to 800 and point --font-sans at it - then delete the Google Fonts link and the two preconnects from _document.tsx. Keep Figtree only as the mono face. Verify at /design-system which section 6.7 names as the regression target.
